title: Zoom in: from one saved event to many inbox entries
caption: The outbox makes publishing reliable, the planner turns one event into bounded jobs, and every write is keyed so it can be replayed.

steps.text: The repo service writes the event and an outbox row in the same transaction: either both exist or neither does.
The relay reads unsent rows, publishes them to the log, and marks a row sent only after the log acknowledges it.
The planner reads the event and asks the watch graph how many watchers the repo has: 40, far below the threshold.
It splits the watcher list into jobs of at most 500 watchers. One job is enough here.
A batch worker appends the event id to each watcher's inbox. The entry key includes the event id, and each list is trimmed to its newest entries.

scenarios.name: Popular repo issue
scenarios.summary: An issue opens on a repo with 250 000 watchers. Watchers get it through the recents, and only the issue's participants get a pushed copy.

steps.text: The planner counts 250 000 watchers, over the threshold.
It writes the event once to the hot-repo recents for read-time merge.
People subscribed to this issue (its author, assignees, those mentioned) are few, so they are still pushed through one normal job.

scenarios.name: Relay crash
scenarios.summary: The relay dies between publishing and marking the row sent. The event is published twice, and the keyed inbox write makes that harmless.

steps.text: The relay publishes a row, then crashes before marking it sent.
On restart it finds the row still unsent and publishes it again: at-least-once, never lost.
The planner makes jobs for both copies. The second write of the same event id to the same inbox replaces the first.

scenarios.name: Stuck batch
scenarios.summary: One job keeps failing because its inbox shard is overloaded. Retries are bounded and the job is parked, so the rest of the queue keeps moving.

steps.text: Writes from one job to an overloaded inbox shard keep timing out.
After three tries with backoff the job goes to the dead-letter queue instead of blocking its worker.
Other jobs, on healthy shards, finish normally. When the shard recovers an operator replays the parked jobs, which is safe because every write is keyed.
